A.explanation: This is about $0.38\%$ of the volume, using the percentage uncertainty in diameter only once instead of three times for $d^3$.

B.explanation: Tripling the $0.38\%$ uncertainty in diameter gives about $1.14\%$ in volume, which is about $0.87\text{ cm}^3$.

C.explanation: This is slightly too large and does not match $3 \times (0.02/5.26) \times 76.2\text{ cm}^3$ when calculated correctly.

D.explanation: This is far too large, about $9\%$ of the volume, and cannot come from a $0.02\text{ cm}$ uncertainty in $5.26\text{ cm}$.

hints: Notice the diameter is $(5.26 \pm 0.02)\text{ cm}$, so first work out the fractional uncertainty $0.02/5.26$ in the diameter.
Recall volume of a sphere is $V = \pi d^3/6$, so $V$ is proportional to $d^3$ and its percentage uncertainty is three times the percentage uncertainty in $d$.
Calculate $V$ from $5.26\text{ cm}$, then find $1.14\%$ of that $V$ to get the absolute uncertainty in $\text{cm}^3$.
walkthrough: Write the volume in terms of diameter: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{\pi d^3}{6}$, so $V$ depends on the third power of the measured $d = 5.26\text{ cm}$.
Find the fractional uncertainty in $d$: $\Delta d/d = 0.02/5.26 \approx 0.00380$, which is a percentage uncertainty of about $0.38\%$.
For a power, multiply the percentage uncertainty by the power: $\Delta V/V = 3 \times \Delta d/d \approx 3 \times 0.38\% \approx 1.14\%$.
Convert to absolute uncertainty: $\Delta V = 0.0114 \times 76.2\text{ cm}^3 \approx 0.87\text{ cm}^3$.
